name: Cultural formulation exploration (original questions; CFI is link-out only)
evidenceLevel: Assessment practice, not a treatment. In the DSM-5 international field trial, patients and clinicians rated the DSM-5 Cultural Formulation Interview (CFI) as feasible, acceptable and clinically useful, and clinicians' feasibility ratings improved after their first interview (Lewis-Fernandez et al., 2017). The CFI is copyrighted by the American Psychiatric Association and is linked out only; the questions in this entry are original and are not the CFI. See DSM-5-TR, Section III: Cultural Formulation.
purpose: A short, respectful conversation to understand how the client's culture, identities, community and life circumstances shape how they experience and explain their distress, how they cope, and what kind of help they want. It draws on explanatory-model ideas (Kleinman, Eisenberg and Good), the ADDRESSING framework (Pamela Hays), and the cultural formulation approach in DSM-5-TR and the ICD-11 clinical descriptions (CDDR). It helps prevent misdiagnosis, improves engagement, and guides how to adapt any intervention in this library. To use the official CFI, its informant version or its supplementary modules, follow the APA link.
steps: Explain why you are asking: you want to understand the client's own view and what matters to them so that care fits. Make clear there are no wrong answers and they can skip any question.
Invite the client to name the problem in their own words, including any family or community term for it (Kleinman's explanatory-model approach).
Explore the client's own explanation: what they think is causing it, what it means for them, and what they fear might happen.

Explore identity and life context using a framework such as Hays' ADDRESSING model (age and generation, developmental and acquired disability, religion, ethnicity, social class, sexual orientation, Indigenous heritage, national origin and gender), plus language, migration and work. Let the client say which parts matter most right now, and ask about discrimination or unfair treatment.
Explore supports and stresses: family, community, faith, work, and how each one helps or adds strain.
Ask about coping and earlier help: what they have tried, including traditional, religious or community healing, and what helped or did not.
Ask about hopes for care and possible barriers: what kind of help they want and from whom, and obstacles such as cost, transport, stigma, language, or mistrust from past experiences.
Name, in your own words, that you and the client may see things differently, and invite correction throughout (cultural humility).
Summarize what you heard and use it to shape goals, interventions and handouts. For the official structured interview, use the APA CFI (link out).
script: You are the expert on your own life. Can you walk me through what has been happening, using whatever words feel right to you?
Is there a name or a saying for this kind of trouble in your family or where you grew up?
What is your own sense of why this started, and why now? People explain these things in many different ways, and all of them are welcome here.
When you picture this getting worse, what scares you the most?

Tell me a little about your world: the people you come from, the communities you are part of, and what daily life is like right now with work, money, health or faith. What in all of that is weighing on you, and what is holding you up?
Have you been treated unfairly because of who you are? How has that affected you?
When life has been hard before, what did you lean on? Who or what made a difference, and did anything make it worse?
If this goes well, what will be different for you a few months from now? And what might make it hard to keep coming? I would rather plan for that now.
I will get some things wrong about your life and your family's ways. When I do, I really want you to tell me.
contraindications: Do not copy, embed or modify the APA Cultural Formulation Interview in this app; it is APA copyrighted. Link out to the official version.
Avoid stereotyping. Culture is personal and changes over time; use the answers to understand this client, not to apply group generalizations.
Use trained professional interpreters, not family members, especially for sensitive topics.

Explanations involving spirits, curses or religious causes are common and are not, on their own, signs of psychosis. Assess within cultural context, and consult cultural brokers or colleagues when unsure.

Do not enter information about immigration status, substance use or other sensitive topics into this tool; nothing is stored or sent. Any export or note about substance use must carry the notice: 42 CFR Part 2 prohibits unauthorized use or disclosure of these records.

This intervention does not assess or decide risk. If suicidal thoughts, self-harm or risk to others come up, follow your setting's risk-assessment and safety-planning procedures. Keep crisis options visible: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US, call or text), the local emergency number, and findahelpline.com for other countries.
culturalAdaptations: Ask about cultural concepts of distress that may apply (for example, ataque de nervios, khyal cap, taijin kyofusho, or 'thinking too much') and what they mean for this person.
Fit the length and order to the setting. A few questions now and more later is better than none.
Include family or community perspectives only with the client's consent. APA also offers an informant version of the CFI (link out).
Treat structural factors such as poverty, racism, housing and legal status as part of the formulation, not only beliefs.
Reflect on your own cultural background, assumptions and power in the room, and practice cultural humility.
